speechtext:
It was made by a committee appointed by the British Columbia section of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in June, 1942. However, no attention was paid to the report, and very little was done about the fuel situation until the month of January, at which time it became clear that the situation was becoming acute.
Let it be noted that despite all efforts to maintain men in the mines, the number of men working, at least in British Columbia mines, has gradually decreased. I hold in my hand a copy of the votes and proceedings for the legislative assembly of British Columbia, under date of February 11, 1943. In this copy I find answers to a series of questions, the first of which was: "How many mine-workers were employed in and around the coal mines of the province of British Columbia in 1930?" There is a further question as to the number for the year 1940, and another as to the number at the present time. The answers are quite revealing, because they show that in 1930 there were 4,645 men employed in and about British Columbia mines. In 1940 that number had dwindled to 2,874, despite the fact that the. demand for coal had greatly increased. In February, 1943, the number had dwindled to 2,365. So that we find that there were approximately twice as many men in British Columbia coal mines in 1930 as there were in 1940 when the demand was very much greater-possibly double that of 1930. Then, the number in 1940 was 500 more than that of 1943. These are facts which indicate what is wrong with the fuel situation at least in British Columbia. It is a condition which cannot be improved merely by tampering with price control structure.
The fuel industry will have to be organized under a competent authority. The whole industry will have to be surveyed to find out the need, and then the labour will have to be made available to meet the need. A difference of opinion arose this afternoon between the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Munitions and Supply with regard to who the members of the fuel control board are. I have here a press release dated March 7, 1943, which states:
Under a new order in council, jurisdiction over the production and supply of coal, coke and wood fuel, has passed from the wartime prices and trade board into the hands of the wartime industries control board, it was announced to-day by the munitions and supply department.

The order in council creates a new coal control, which will assume the powers, duties, and functions of the coal administration, including the continued operation of the dominion fuel board, which was absorbed by the coal administration in 1941. All supply orders issued by the administration have become orders of the coal control.
The staffs of the coal administration and of the dominion fuel board have been transferred to the munitions and supply department. James McGregor Stewart, K.C., is now coal controller and will retain his title and powers as coal administrator, under which he will continue to regulate prices of coal, coke, and wood fuel. Frank G. Neate, who has been deputy coal administrator, is now deputy coal controller. D. Roy Cameron, formerly deputy administrator (wood fuel), and Gustave C. Piche, of Quebec and Montreal, a forestry engineer and formerly chief of the forest service for the province of Quebec, have been appointed as deputy wood fuel controllers.
It seems to me that the hon. member for Cape Breton South is rather better informed on. this matter than the two ministers.

Mr. Speaker, coming as I do from the province of Nova Scotia and the county of Cumberland I am interested in this discussion, from the point of view of both production and consumption. Both the province of Nova Scotia and the county of Cumberland are exporters of coal, but notwithstanding this fact they have problems with respect to getting supplies to heat their homes and keep the industries going. There are two large coal fields in Cumberland county, Springhill field and River Hebert-Joggins. I have not the exact figures, but we produce annually in the county about three quarters of a million tons of coal. I believe that if this industry had been properly organized and the skilled miners retained, we could have enlarged the production beyond 750,000 tons of coal and we would be producing a million tons.
Since the commencement of hostilities, the mines of Cumberland and Nova Scotia have been greatly handicapped on account of a

Fuel Shortage-Mr. Black (Cumberland)
shortage of skilled man-power. I agree with what the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has said with respect to the enlistment of miners who could have served their country better in the mines than in the armed forces, but I disagree with him in one respect. I do not believe the miners from the county of Cumberland enlisted because they wanted to get away from the coal mines. They enlisted from a sense of duty to their country; they enlisted voluntarily to serve in any theatre of war.
Some time ago 500 experienced miners had enlisted from the Springhill mines. I assume that the total figure is now 600 or 700. These mines require a daily working force of about 1,250 miners to carry on their present scale of production, but they have 1,600 to 1,700 on their payrolls. Many of the men are not experienced coal miners, and their morale has not been kept up as it should have been. The same condition applies in the River Hebert-Joggins field. In this district the mines are smaller and the seams are thinner, but I believe the percentage of enlistments has been as large as that from any part of Canada. These men also volunteered to serve in any theatre of war. The output of the mines has been reduced and the cost has been increased. If a proper policy of selective service had been put into effect early in the war, or were put into effect even now, it would have gone a long way in solving this fuel problem.
I referred to the morale of the miners in Cumberland and throughout Nova Scotia. This has not been what it should be, but I do not blame them. There- has been dissatisfaction with regard to taxation, and this should have been avoided. However, most of the miners continued to work irrespective of the incidence of taxation. A single man begins to pay income taxes when he has earned $660, and a married man at $1,200, and they continue to work with hesitancy and without the goodwill they should have. When these earnings are exceeded almost 100 per cent is applied to taxation, and this leaves a bad taste.
Perhaps hon. members may have noticed in the press that the miners in Springhill have lately not been able to get coal which they mine themselves to heat their own homes. The coal had been assigned for shipment elsewhere. If things were properly handled, a condition such as this would not exist. The miners of the county of Cumberland and the province of Nova Scotia are willing and ready to do their duty, but they will not stand for injustice or unfair treatment.
There was also a feeling of resentment when the Minister of Munitions and Supply, (Mr. Howe), when he was Minister of Transport, converted the steamship Charlottetown from the burning of coal to the burning of oil without any explanation to the people of the coal producing communities which depended upon this for about 25,000 tons a year to give them a home market for their product. There was also resentment in connection with rationing because the miners felt that they should have been allowed larger quantities of food and beverages in their hazardous occupation. If they were satisfied that restrictions were necessary, they would willingly submit to them.
I agree with what the hon. member for Cape Breton South has said about the resentment over the fact that our coal mining districts have had no representative on the fuel board. The coal miners of our province would have more confidence in government policy if there were a representative of theirs on the fuel board. There are in that province a number of capable and experienced practical men who have the confidence of the coal miners. I was in the government at Halifax for eight years or more, and there was never a major matter having to do with the coal mining industry or labour when we did not consult the miners. On many occasions I came to Ottawa in connection with the payment of subventions which resulted in extending the market for Nova Scotia coal. We always consulted the heads of the miners' organizations, and on -many occasions we asked them to accompany us and assist us in making our presentation to the government or to the fuel board and those in authority. In that way we obtained their good-will, and that feeling spread among the workmen in the industry. Had the government followed that policy and given our miners representation, it would have assisted in building up the morale of the miners in Nova Scotia and greatly helped the coal industry.
We have some capable men on the fuel board. Those of us in Nova Scotia who contended for many years for expansion of the Canadian market for our coal will be forever grateful to those responsible for putting our coal subvention policies into effect in central Canada. The man perhaps more helpful than any other is Mr. Frank Neate, who is now deputy coal administrator. The late hon. Wesley Gordon, at that time minister of mines, did us a fine service in approving a national fuel policy and appropriating large sums of money in order that we might market an additional tonnage of Nova Scotia coal in central Canada. It was our policy at that time
Fuel Shortage-Mrs. Nielsen

to establish a market within Canada, for a minimum of seven million tons of coal a year. We had to extend our territory from Montreal as far west as Toronto in order to market that output, but to-day we are supplying a market only as far west as Levis. A long educational process was required to teach the people of central Canada to fit their boilers for the use of Nova Scotia coal. That will have to be done over again. Nova Scotia, in view of all the sacrifices made in confederation, contends that it is entitled to that market, and the coal mines of Nova Scotia should be kept operating, in the years after the war, in supplying that market.
We have now on the fuel board Mr. J. McG. Stewart, Iv.C., from Nova Scotia. It is true that he is a lawyer, but he is a very able man and has done excellent service for the benefit not only of Nova Scotia and all Canada as chairman of the fuel board.

I realize that so much has been said on the subject before the house that there is very little one can add, but I feel that the situation in Saskatchewan should be brought to the attention of the minister. I do not agree, however, with the last speaker (Mr. Soper), when he stated that what has occured here to-day will cause "serious consequences in the months to come, in that fuel will be hoarded; for the fact is that a month ago or less the minister himself put an announcement before the country to the effect that if something were not done, serious consequences would follow next winter. What the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) has done is to rivet the attention of the country on the fuel situation and the necessity of action being taken now and has given the members of the house an opportunity to suggest what should be done.
As far as Saskatchewan is concerned, the government was warned last fall by the city of Prince Albert, which is represented in this house by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), that serious consequences would follow unless something were done to assure a reasonable production of wood fuel in the area in the vicinity of Prince Albert. The wartime prices and trade board fixed the price of fuel wood in Saskatchewan on a 1941 basic price level, at which time the price of cord-wood in Saskatchewan was scarcely higher than it had been during the years of the

Fuel Shortage-Mr. Diejenbaker
depression, when the getting out of cordwood was a means whereby many settlers were able to assure themselves of a livelihood.
Take, for instance, the price of poplar wood. A man working reasonably hard can get out two cords a day. For that he received wages of four dollars, or two dollars a cord, out of which he had to pay to the provincial government stumpage fees of twenty cents a cord, or forty cents. The return was so low that the settlers would not get out wood for sale.
They could not get any help and if they did get it out they were working at a wage far below that paid by lumber industries in the far west and in northern Ontario. As a matter of fact most men who previously got out wood in Saskatchewan went to northern Ontario where they received $4.80 for a double cord of pulpwood, and had their fare paid both ways. There was no incentive whatever for anyone to produce w'ood in Saskatchewan. In the fall of 1942 the wartime prices and trade board was asked by the city of Prince Albert, and I believe a like communication was made to the Prime Minister as member for that constituency, that prices should be fixed at a level which would assure those engaged in the production of wood of a reasonable wage. The prices suggested were, $6 for poplar, $6.50 for jackpine and $8 for tamarac. But the wartime prices and trade board refused to do anything in that connection, although in Kenora in northern Ontario, for like wood, 87.50, $8.50 and $10 were the prices permitted to be paid.
The situation in Saskatchewan having been brought to the notice of the government in the fall of 1942, the government must assume the responsibility for the shortage that occurred in January and February, 1943. If fuel conditions in Vancouver, where the climate is so balmy, caused the discomfort referred to by several hon. members, the situation in Saskatchewan during the past winter can be imagined. In Prince Albert for a period of ten days forty per cent of the population had little or no fuel; yet adjacent to Prince Albert and throughout northern Saskatchewan are vast fuel resources uncut for the reason that there was no selective service system that would put men out to cut this wood; uncut because it was not profitable for the farmers or settlers to get it out and because it was impossible to secure men to work at wage levels lower than those paid in British Columbia and northern Ontario for similar work.
I have three suggestions to offer to the minister. These have come to me from vari-

ous settlers in northern Saskatchewan who believe they would assure an ample supply of the necessary wood during the coming winter.
1.	The dollar subsidy, if I may call it that, paid to the dealers will not meet the situation, because it will not be passed back to the producers. The subsidy should be paid direct to the producer, the settler, the farmer, or the labourer as the case may be.
2.	The dominion government in order to encourage production should pay the provincial stumpage fees.
3.	There are any number of farmers living in northern Saskatchewan in the wooded areas who would be very glad to get out wood if they had the necessary finances or financial assistance to enable them to do so. I suggest that the government finance the farmers by advancing a portion of the price of the wood once it has been placed on the skidways. That will enable the farmer to get and to pay the nece'ssary help, and the remainder of the purchase price would be paid to him at the time he makes delivery.
4.	The Indian reservations in Saskatchewan afford an opportunity to get man-power for this work. There are not as many adult men on these reserves as their were a few years ago, for the Indians have made a contribution to this country, have given an example of service, unequalled by any other race. I think every able-bodied man in every reserve in Saskatchewan, certainly those in northern Saskatchewan, has volunteered. But those who are at home on the reserves, if they were given an opportunity to earn money by getting out wood, would do so, provided .that their earnings were turned over to them, not handled through the Indian department or the Indian agencies, I have it on good authority that there are at least 700 to 800 men, Indians, both on and off the reserves in the northern part of Saskatchewan, who are available to go out and cut wood.
I believe that unless something is done immediately, the fuel situation in Saskatchewan next winter will be a desperate one.
A similar shortage in production prevails in the lumbering industry. The labour is not available, because the government has not seen fit to direct men into the service that they should serve in, and has given them freedom to go from one part of Canada to another where wages are highest. Our labourers, lumber producers and the like will not stay in northern Saskatchewan producing lumber and fuelwood when the wages there are about half of what they can get in British Columbia or northern Ontario. They go where the wages

Fuel Shortage-Mr. Shaiv
are best. In the production of fuel the government can carry into practical application the recent orders in council that, as the hon. member for Vancouver Bast (Mr. Maclnnis) *said, promised that much would be done, that look well on paper, but are not being properly carried into effect.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of the afternoon a number of hon. members engaged in the debate on the very important subject of fuel, and dealt with the conditions which prevailed earlier in the present winter and the conditions that may well be anticipated in future should there not be some radical change in policy with respect to the handling of the fuel question. My colleague the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) reminded the house that if other groups or political parties in this country had adopted the same attitude toward the manpower question that we adopted in 1939 and 1940, and in fact still hold, many of the troubles which now confront us never would have occurred. I say that if other political parties had not spent their time in what I call political tomfoolery, probably there would have been no necessity for the conglomeration of regulations which emanate from government offices almost every week, and which serve to do little more than further confuse us. The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Soper) attributed a good deal of our uneasiness to pessimism, if I interpreted his words correctly. I understand he is a dealer and incidentally a consumer; but evidently he has very little faith in his own Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), who indicated through the press that there was all the reason in the world for pessimism under the present government policy.
It seems rather strange that I, coming from the province of Alberta where we produce approximately eighty-five per cent of Canada's coal, and from a constituency in which there is a number of mines producing domestic coal, should have to take part in a debate of this kind on account of the fact that in my own constituency a good deal of hardship was caused by the acute shortage of fuel. So great was that shortage; so difficult were the problems which confronted a great many of the people of Red Deer constituency, that upon returning to this house in January I felt obliged to place upon the order paper a resolution, which I should like to read:
Whereas domestic fuel is a vital necessity in Canadian homes;
And whereas the acute shortage of domestic fuel available for home consumption has created severe hardship and in many instances acute suffering in many parts of Canada during the present winter;
Therefore be it resolved,-That, in the opinion of this house, parliament should immediately take such steps as are considered necessary to bring into production and distribution undeveloped fuel resources of Canada.
That resolution may appear rather restricted in its application. If I had been given an opportunity to sponsor the resolution, I would not have confined myself merely to the development and distribution of undeveloped resources; but having seen the figures of the estimated coal requirements in Canada, I was concerned about this fact, namely, that the sources of supply which had been developed could not, in my opinion, supply the needs. I do not intend to elaborate upon that resolution at this time. If I were sponsoring it, I would feel obliged to take the .forty minutes at my disposal.
During the past winter, in the city of Red Deer particularly, acute hardships were experienced; in fact I am almost obliged to believe that the Minister of Munitions and Supply was referring to Red Deer or the residents of that city when he made reference to the fact that some people had burned their fences. I know that as a result of the shortage of fuel there the schools were closed and a great many business establishments either closed or nearly closed; and when I speak thus I do not confine my remarks merely to Red Deer but include many different towns in that constituency. Furthermore I know the situation became so acute that the two airports in that vicinity were contemplating either closing entirely or at least curtailing their operations.
The people of Red Deer were perturbed. The people of the other towns of my constituency were also rather disturbed. I must pay tribute to the dealers who in a splendid manner adopted a scheme of rationing, but I do not believe that responsibility should be placed on the dealers, for it put them in a very nasty position, if I may use that word.
Mr. HANSELL; You may.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Thank you. A number of factors were responsible for the acute fuel shortage. I will not attempt for a moment to minimize the fact that we had a very severe winter, but as yet we have had no communique from anywhere indicating that next winter will be any milder. In fact, in war time, whatever the cause, we seem to encounter more severe weather than during
Fuel Shortage-Mr. Shaw

peace time. I will not try to elaborate upon that; I could not. In any event we in Red Deer were confronted with a serious problem in regard to transportation. As I say, we have numerous small mines in that district, but there was difficulty in securing the trucks necessary to move the coal. The coal was available, but there was greatly reduced production by reason of the insufficient number of miners available to keep those mines operating to capacity.
May I point out that there are a number of reasons why our truckers have difficulty in carrying on the hauling of coal. In the first place they are having a much harder time in procuring parts for their machines. They have difficulty in obtaining tires-and I am not complaining about this unnecessarily, because it is a situation which confronts us. Not only that, but many of our truckers have * been directed to other places as a result of the higher rates of remuneration to be found in those places. I have in mind particularly the large numbers of truckers who accepted work on the Alaska highway. I know, further, that the Canadian Pacific Railway was undoubtedly confronted with problems in connection with transportation. I am told that freight cars loaded with coal stood near the mines for days and days, and could not be moved. I do not know the exact reason for this, but I can surmise as to what it may be.
With respect to the actual production of coal, to the best of my knowledge none of the mines has closed in that constituency on account of a shortage of man-power. I know that many smaller mines in Alberta have closed down completely because the miners have been taken or have gone elsewhere. As I said, that is to a degree responsible for the situation. Many of our men engaged in the mining industry volunteered for service in the army, the air force and the navy. They were encouraged to do so. Probably they received that encouragement from a spirit of adventure. Probably they were encouraged by more attractive employment, as has already been explained to-day.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Give them some credit for patriotism, too.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I think I am about the last one in the world who would cast any reflection upon the patriotism of any young man. Many of these men joined the service voluntarily; many of them were taken under the provisions of the National Resources Mobilization Act, and many others have taken employment in other branches of war industry because mine operators could not compete, from the point 
of view of wages, with the operators of other industries engaged in the production of war commodities.
Prom experience I know of the extreme difficulty with which many of us were confronted when we endeavoured to procure leaves of absence for some of the miners who were taken into the army under the National Resources Mobilization Act. I do not believe the government appreciated the situation. I will not try to determine the reason for that; but surely they should have had the facilities at their disposal to determine whether or not an individual was actually required in the coal mines, or somewhere else. But we went on for weeks and weeks and weeks until we have become sick and tired of the whole thing.
In order to conserve the time of the house I do not propose to elaborate upon these matters at any greater length. Let me come now to the question of wood. I am in absolute agreement with the hon. member who said this afternoon that we should give consideration to subsidizing the actual producer of wood-if "subsidizing" is the proper word. In my constituency the farmers in their spare time engaged in the cutting of wood. That is what they used to do, but now most of their labour has been taken, and as a result they have no spare time. When they had the spare time, however, they engaged in the cutting of firewood, and hauled it to town for sale. We have our dealers in the towns, too; but in my part of Alberta, in the smaller urban and rural areas, they constitute a small minority. I say we should give consideration to the subsidizing of those farmers, so that they will be encouraged to cut fuel and deliver it to the towns. Some of them have told me recently that it is not worth their while, and that they will not bother with it any more. In a sense, I do not blame them; and yet that course will not solve our fuel problems. On the other hand, I would urge that there be a redirection of miners from the armed services and from other branches of industry back to the mines. That is an absolute essential.
The question of the division of responsibility arises. My opinion in this connection is based to a great extent upon the statement of the Minister of Munitions and Supply that we shall have a fight between the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipal districts. It will be most unfortunate if the federal government fails to recognize its responsibility in this regard.

Fuel Shortage-Mr. Black (Yukon)
The solution of our fuel problem will not come through these three bodies fighting until such time as the next winter is upon us.
There is another matter with which I should like to deal in conclusion. We still have 22,000 gold miners engaged in the production of gold in Canada. I know this is a touchy question in the minds of some people, but I would remind the house that the President of the United States showed courage when he dealt with it. I reminded the house on March 1 that a committee of the house of representatives had stated that it would not be the better part of wisdom for the United States even to contemplate the acceptance of gold after this war as a method of settling debts as between the United States and other countries.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: But they are still producing gold.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: True; but it will be noticed that the action taken in the United States is far more drastic than was ever contemplated before.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: They produced more last year than the year before.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to give me the date upon which the President issued his most recent order.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I cannot keep track of those dates.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Then why ask me to? I trust there is no scheme being concocted to put us back on the gold standard. I am of opinion, and there are medical men in the house who could confirm my opinion, that it is now realized it is not the best thing for one's health to put gold in his teeth. This all leads to a more limited commercial use of the commodity. I am of opinion, one which is held by many people throughout the country, that the 22,000 skilled miners engaged in the production of gold should be put to work producing something which has been proven to be of far greater value in wartime, namely, coal.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
know the difference between a hard-rock miner and a soft-coal miner?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Under the present policy the government is placing the men in such a position that if the mines are to carry on, and supply even part of our needs, they will have to take workers who have not the skill or the adaptability that these 22,000 gold miners would have.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
know that coal mining is a highly skilled employment? In some provinces there are regulations an individual has to pass before he can work in a coal mine.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
The point is that they have to be trained, in any event. I ask the Minister of Labour where he will get the men who must be directed to the production of coal in order to meet the requirements of this country. I say that we can take a miner engaged in gold mining and train him for that purpose much easier and in a shorter time than we can many of those upon whom he may have his eyes at the present time.
I realized before I mentioned that subject that it would be a touchy matter with some people, but it will be noticed that in the light of that I did not refrain from mentioning it. I contend that unless we give sound consideration forthwith to the whole man-power question-after all, this is part of the manpower question-we shall shortly be confronted with difficulties which few anticipate at the present time. I know that some will say I am a pessimist. I would sooner be a pessimist and avoid a terrible situation that might come along later on than be an extreme optimist, or, in other words, an ostrich, burying my head in the sand and hoping and praying that everything will work out satisfactorily. We have had altogether too much of that up to the present time.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Especially from the Liberal side of the house.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The hon. member for Macleod says that that is especially so from across the floor on the government side of the house. I agree.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate which has taken place this afternoon on the shortage of fuel, particularly wood fuel, reminds me of that old rhyme, "How much wood would a woodchuck chuck, if a woodchuck could chuck wrood." I think this applies particularly to the remarks of the speaker (Mr. Shaw) who has just preceded me. It may seem strange that we should have a fuel shortage in the Yukon, but this is due, to some extent, to war conditions. Those in the Yukon who owned trucks and tractors and who would ordinarily be engaged in the transportation of fuel, have for the most part leased or sold them to contractors on the Alaska highway, thereby doing much better for themselves than if they had continued to use their machines. In addition, many of the men who would be

Fuel Shortage-Mr. Black (Yukon)
engaged in this industiy have volunteered for active service with the army, the navy or the air force.
Under an agreement between the governments of the United States and Canada, Canadian workmen are prevented from obtaining employment with United States contractors and earning the splendid wages paid United States workmen. I protested against this policy as being wholly unfair to Canadian workmen, but it is still in effect. Some Canadian workmen have been clever enough to find a way around this prohibition, and they are cutting poles for these contractors. I know of one expert Canadian axeman who cleared $135 in one day. One could not expect that man to cut wood for fuel when a ceiling of from seventy-five cents to $1 an hour was put on his wages by the labour board. As I say, the Canadian fuel shortage is due, to some extent, to war conditions, and also to the administration of the selective service policy.
I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) one instance that came to my notice recently. A group of young men were trained as welders in a Winnipeg trades school and were sent by the selective service bureau at Winnipeg to Toronto to report to the selective service bureau there. Immediately upon arrival at Toronto they were told that they were urgently needed at Transcona and would have to leave at once. When they said that they had just come from there the Ontario selective service officer said to them, "No; you came from Winnipeg and we are sending you to Transcona." Evidently the official in the selective service bureau at Winnipeg did not know that welders were needed at Transcona, while the official in the selective service bureau at Toronto did not seem to know that Transcona is practically a part of Winnipeg and that the workmen go back and forth daily between Winnipeg and Transcona. Surely the Minister of Labour does not approve such stupidity on the part of his officials. I suggest that he supply them with geographies.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: If what my hon. friend is saying is true, I should like to have the details. It seems almost incredible.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
If the Minister of Labour will apply to his own selective service bureaus at Winnipeg and at Toronto he will get the information officially. We hear about the overcrowding of railway trains. Why overcrowd a railway car to send a crowd of men from Winnipeg to Toronto and then back again to Winnipeg?

In the Yukon we have no draft evaders, no conscientious objectors, no prisoners of war, no Doukhobors and no slackers, and we do not need any regimentation of labour. If the men there were allowed a fair wage for their work, they would get out the fuel. I say to the Minister of Labour that if he is so inclined he can solve the difficulty as far as the Yukon is concerned.
Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South): Mr. Speaker, I intend to take only two or three minutes-

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I knew that would be pleasing to the house. That is the best cheer I have got since I came to the House of Commons. There is a suggestion which I wish to make to the minister, and there is something which I should like to draw to his attention and which I think will at least help in solving the fuel problem in western Ontario.
In the first place may I preface my remarks by saying that this is definitely the government's responsibility, it cannot be placed upon the municipalities. Under the expansion of war services the dominion government have taken charge of practically every provincial organization. They have taken charge of the administration of timber, mines and everything else that ordinarily would come under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments.
In western Ontario we have a very serious situation with regard to gas and oil fuel. On several occasions I brought this matter up in the house. For a year and a half there was a rather vacillating policy; nothing definite was done, and the result was that many people in western Ontario suffered serious hardships and went to tremendous expense to remove the gas-burners from their furnaces and put in coal burners and other methods of burning fuel.
It was felt that the wealthy gas companies, controlled principally in the United States, should have been compelled to reimburse the people for the expenses to which they had gone. Either that, or the government should have reimbursed them for the hundreds and hundreds of dollars they had spent in taking out of gas fixtures and rebuilding their chimneys in order to burn some other type of fuel. But that was not done, and in a part of the country where over ten per cent of the men have volunteered to go to war, we perhaps do not criticize as vehemently as we might some of the regulations put out by the government.
The other day the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Cardiff) brought a letter to my attention because we had been discussing the

Fuel Shortage-Mr. Homuth
fuel situation only a day or so before, and I wish to read this letter to the minister and suggest that a great deal more of the cooperative spirit that is evident in this letter might well be shown in our war effort. The letter reads as follows:
Harrison, March 10, 1943.
Mr. E. Cardiff, M.P.,
Brussels, Ontario.
Dear friend:
I am writing you for information and advice, re the subsidy on fuel wood.
About February 1st a number of my neighbours who have no wood or bush of their own asked me to sell them firewood.
We have made a bargain whereby for every cord of firewood they cut and draw away they cut a cord for me. I am very proud of the way it is working. We have men from the village going in with farmers who have horses to do the hauling. We have had as many as 10 men and 4 teams working at once.
Now I think I am entitled to the $1 per cord subsidy, on all the fuel wood which is hauled away from my bush. There is no wood dealer involved in the whole transaction. No money is paid for the wood dr for labour excepting to the man who operates the buzz-saw.
I do not think I am entitled to the subsidy on the wood which I keep and burn in my own home. I would be pleased to hear from you and have your opinion.
I know for a fact these men are not worrying about their supply of firewood for next winter, as we have about 120 cords cut already.
Yours truly,
Milton Leonard,
R.R. No. 2, Harrison, Ont.
That shows a spirit of cooperation which could be built up in Canada if the government would only go out and build it up. We have built thousands of homes across this country, war-time houses that are supposed to be wrecked when the war is over, but if we had carried on a campaign which would have aroused in the people a sense of their responsibility and of that patriotism of which they are capable it would not have been necessary to build a great many of these homes. We could have found many homes with rooms that are not occupied and many others which could have been subdivided, but the whole war-time housing programme was conducted through a series of newspaper advertisements, which must have cost a great deal of money, and nothing substantial came of it all. Surely the members of this house and the people of this country are prepared to carry on a campaign to stir up the patriotism of our people. Look at the tremendous number of war-time houses that have been built in the city of Hamilton, or in the city of Galt, in my riding, where fifty are being built now. If a campaign had been carried
on to arouse the patriotism of the people, they would have opened their homes and taken people in, and these war-time houses would not have been required.
Similarly we could carry on a campaign to stimulate the cutting of wood fuel. There is no part of western Ontario that has not a good acreage of bush from which wood fuel could be cut. All that is required to stimulate production is cooperation. The writer of the letter I have read cannot get the subsidy. I called up the fuel controller's office and was told that under the order in council this man cannot get the subsidy. Why? Because he is not a dealer. Surely, Mr. Speaker, a man who is willing to sacrifice his bush and keep down the price of winter fuel ought to be entitled to the subsidy at least on that part of his fuel which goes to other homes than his own. Unfortunately, so many of these orders in council are drawn up by men who cannot see and have not seen or will not see the practical side of some of these problems. The hon. member for Huron North and I talked with Mr. Cameron, and he said, "It is a matter of administration. But the order in council does not provide for paying subsidy in this case." I believe that if the minister would advise his board to go out and try to build up some of the cooperative spirit shown by the writer of this, letter, a great deal could be done to alleviate the fuel shortage across Canada. There is on the part of everybody in this country a spirit of cooperation and a desire to help the war effort. But these silly orders in council and these crazy regulations which make a man so dizzy that he does not know where he stands break down the desire on the part of the people to do something in the war effort. I point out to the minister that much can be done, not only in this fuel situation, but in connection with housing and many other problems that face the government if they would just approach the people in the proper way, explain the situation to them, appeal to their patriotism and be honest with them. There is no question that the people would cooperate heartily.
The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Soper) this afternoon said that this was an idle debate which would cause a run on fuel. Let me point out to him that every time any of the controllers appointed by this government announces that there will be no control or rationing of this or that commodity, the people immediately go out and buy it. Why? Because they cannot believe the controllers. They know that the controllers say in February, there will be no control-and in March control
Fuel Shortage-Mr. Pouliot

goes on. The controllers say in January, there will be no rationing-and in February rationing goes on. And so it goes. What we must have in this country is a spirit of cooperation, and I wish to tell the government that the people are prepared to cooperate with the government if the government is prepared to cooperate with them.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question is a very important one. The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) and the premiers of the various provinces have often, in interviews given to the press, drawn the attention of the public to the importance of the fuel problem. In our part of the country coal is imported from other provinces and from some of the eastern United States. But most people use wood for fuel, hardwood like maple, the wild cherry tree, birch and other varieties which are most suitable for making the homes of our fellow-citizens warm and comfortable.
It has been suggested by some of the members that a subsidy should be paid to the farmers to encourage them to cut wood for fuel. Of course, it is a work that requires experience. No novice can pick up an axe and go out into the bush and cut down trees and split wood, but in our part of the country there is not a single farmer or a farmer's son who cannot do that kind of work. They are all familiar with it; they are expert woodcutters.
Some one has complained of the number of Canadian woodsmen who are working in the United States. The main reason is obvious, it is that we have reached a point, mostly on account of forest fires, when United States forests supply some Canadian mills along the border.
But there is another reason why Canadians cross the boundary to chop lumber in the United States; it is because over there they pay fair wages, considerably higher than those which are paid by some companies, one of which operates in my county. It is not at all surprising that young men or older men refuse to work for a company which pays so much less by the hour or by the contract than do the United States companies.
Is this the right time to offer a subsidy for cutting lumber? We know that the time to cut trees is when there is no sap in them. Spring will start, officially, on March 21. We have at times spells of cold weather, but the sap is about to run in the trees. It will then be too late to cut them.
One reason for the present scarcity of lumber is the very large quantity of snow which has fallen in our forests and which has made the cutting of trees more difficult.

The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) spoke of the labour board; and in this matter we have every reason to complain of the wartime prices board, because, by making public a certain price which has been established for kindling wood and for furnace wood, they have removed all possibility for those who look after the transportation of that wood from the forest to the homes of the people to continue that work. The price has been published. The producer asked for the price which was originally paid' by the consumer, and the middleman has nothing at all wherewith to pay for transportation. These regulations have been made by men who are bookworms and who have no experience in the lumber trade, particularly in that regard. By trying to improve conditions they have made the situation much worse than it was.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) made some apt remarks about the difficulty of transportation by trucks. I will not repeat what he has so accurately enumerated, but this is a great difficulty which is not easy to remedy. Then, of course, there are also the railways. But at the present time the railways are jammed. It has been remarked that anyone who travels from Toronto to Montreal, or who goes to St. Lambert, near Montreal, will see all the sidings full of war material which was made a year or two ago and which has not been moved. It would be a great help if that material, whether munitions, aeroplanes, or otherwise, could be forwarded to Russia, the United Kingdom, China, wherever it is needed, but it is left here to rot. We hope that it will not be destroyed completely. But it is in boxes and cases; rain and snow have been falling on it for years, and now what is being done? Those boxes and cases are being painted. But it is too late. Would it have been easier to transport fuel than it has proved to be to carry that mass of munitions which we see on all the sidings in eastern Canada?
The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) who for such a long time has been advocating total war, recited as his own this afternoon part of an article which I wrote in French and which was entitled, " Elliott Little was Right." Does he suffer from amnesia? I remember the time, which is not so far distant, when he insisted on sending all our young men to Libya. He blamed the government for not sending young Canadians to Libya; he wanted conscription for overseas at once. And now we see a number of these champions of conscription for overseas service asking the government not to apply conscription to the army. If they complain about something, they may weep for their own sins. We have

Fuel Shortage-Mr. Pouliot
heard hon. gentlemen opposite rising in their places one after another asking for the conscription of all men for the army.

Mr. Speaker, serious as the fuel situation in Canada appears to be, I certainly hope for the good of the Canadian people that it is not as serious as it has been represented to this house this afternoon and evening. Certain contributory factors to our present fuel situation should be taken into consideration. There has undoubtedly been underproduction, particularly of coal. I well remember deputations coming here from the east and from the west last spring and summer asking why the coal

miners could work for only two or three days a week. Yet apparently no solution of that problem was found.
There are other factors over which not even the Liberal government with its safe majority has much control. As already pointed out, we have had a very severe winter. I do not know how other members have fared, but I have personally just about gone bankrupt paying for coal. There are still other factors. There has been a great demand for manpower. It is quite evident that we cannot have a man in the armed forces, working in agriculture, working in a munitions factory, and at the same time cutting wood or digging coal. There is also this factor, that we have in the past depended to a large extent upon men who were living near the margin of subsistence to dig our coal and chop our wood. To-day these men are able to find employment at better wages elsewhere and are not anxious to dig coal or chop wood.
The question has been raised regarding the effect of the wartime prices and trade board regulations upon the fuel situation. I suggest that the root of the trouble as far as the wartime prices and trade board is concerned has not yet been mentioned in this house. To my mind it is this, that the regulations laid down by that board have in almost every instance militated against the primary producer and the small dealer. That has been brought out, I think, though it has not been specifically mentioned in the debate this afternoon and evening. We have learned that the primary producers of both wood and coal in New Brunswick, northern Saskatchewan and British Columbia were being underpaid and found it unprofitable to work in the production of fuel in competition with other lines of industry.
Last year I was approached by the retail coal dealers' association in Toronto, and it was pointed out to me at that time that more than one hundred small coal dealers in that city were forced out of business on account of government regulations and restrictions which favoured the big coal dealers in that city. I discussed that matter on numerous occasions with the coal administrator, ^ and a special committee was sent to^ investigate the situation in Toronto. Our claim was that if these small dealers were forced out of business, there would not be sufficient equipment to deliver coal to the people of that city during the coming winter. The investigator who went to Toronto reported to me later that he was satisfied that the remaining coal dealers were quite capable of delivering all the coal that would require to be delivered in

Toronto during the following winter, and that no danger would result from large numbers of the small dealers being forced out of business. I maintain that our fuel situation, in so far as the wartime prices and trade board affects the situation, is caused by the fact that its regulations, unintentionally or otherwise, in every instance have favoured the big business man.
It has been the practice to-day to offer suggestions to the minister. I wish to offer one that I know he will not accept any more than he will accept any of the others that have already been offered. My suggestion is that the minister follow the example of the United States government and send every one of these dollar-a-year men, who are to-day being paid by big business, back to the firms from which they came. They found they had to do that in the United States. Those whom they retained as dollar-a-year men they retained only in an advisory capacity, and not in administrative posts. If the minister will surround himself, not by men recruited from big business who have the outlook and the point of view of big business only, but with some who know the needs and have the outlook of the common primary producers, the small business men and the small dealers of this country, and will take their advice occasionally, we shall not get into such a muddle regarding our fuel problem.
Mr. MARK C. SENN (Haldimand): Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a phase of the fuel situation which has not so far been discussed. It is true that it is somewhat of a local character and of local interest, but none the less it is important.
In the district from which I come and throughout all southern Ontario we have a fuel known as natural gas. It is used in the heating of homes, for cooking and also for lighting in a great many places, particularly where we have no hydro facilities. This gas is used not only in farm homes but in towns and villages, and is distributed in the larger centres such as Hamilton, Brantford, St. Catharines and so on.
This gas, as the house well knows, is produced from wells running anywhere from 600 to 1,200 feet in depth. The wells are put down by large drilling outfits which are operated by skilled labour, and each well costs anywhere from $800 to 51,500. Therefore the house will readily understand that the average farmer cannot himself finance such an operation.
The development is, of course, carried on by companies and syndicates, whose progress is seriously retarded for two reasons. First, there is the labour shortage. I can tell the minister of at least two large drilling outfits in my particular neighbourhood which are lying idle because the skilled labour that was operating them has been conscripted or taken into the army. The other reason, of which I would ask the minister to take particular note, is a shortage of gas pipe and casing for the wells. This material is, of course, made of iron or steel, and is very difficult to obtain at the present time, with the result that the development of these gas fields is being seriously delayed. Most of the operations take place during the summer months. It may be said that there will be little need of extra gas for fuel during the remainder of the winter or through out the summer; but if we are to have the operations expanded and the developments carried on, the work will be seriously affected if we have not some priorities for gas pipe and for the casings which are put into the well.
The supervision of this gas business has been carried on almost wholly by the provincial mining department. There has been a gas controller in our province for a great many years. However, last fall an order went out, I believe from the wartime prices and trade board, at least from the fuel administrator, disallowing the use of natural gas in furnaces. Many people were put to a good deal of trouble to re-equip their furnaces. In many instances they were unable to do so. Wood stoves and coal stoves are very difficult to buy at the moment, and their scarcity has caused many people a good deal of trouble in changing from the one sort of fuel to the other. After all, this gas fuel takes the place of coal and wood. It is very important in that particular district and, in fact, all through southern Ontario. I draw this matter to the attention of the minister because, if anything can be done to enable the companies which are developing these fields to get supplies, it would be of great assistance to the fuel situation in that particular district.
Fuel Shortage-Mr. McGarry

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Although the matter I wish to deal with is substantially of a local nature, it is quite relevant to the subject under discussion.
In Port Hood, in my constituency, the people have been subjected to a serious shortage of fuel, and have suffered considerably as a consequence; and this, despite the fact that within the precincts of the town is a large block of coal, which is easily accessible, and which dould be economically mined. A cooperative company which has in mind the opening of this mine would receive sufficient financial stimulus from the provincial government to start operations. An appeal has been made to the fuel controller, Mr. Stewart, but up to the present time nothing has been done: the request to open the mine has not been granted. In view of the conditions which prevail locally, the shortage of coal, the suffering entailed upon the people of Port Hood as a consequence, and the great cry which is heard now regarding the national shortage of coal, and in view of the fact that there is here a splendid block of coal which could be economically mined, and that there are enough men over military age in the town to do the work, it seems to me that it is rather senseless, and a demonstration neither of compassion nor of interest in the war effort to leave this block of coal unworked.
In the town of Inverness the largest producer has become somewhat reduced in volume, so that the production is not as great as it was some years ago. But there are in that area several seams which could be mined very economically and would produce large quantities of coal. I understand that the provincial government has in mind assistance for the opening and developing of some of these seams, but the retarding agency, as far as I can learn, is the fuel controller.
Last fall fifty per cent of the assessable property in the town of Port Hood was swept away by fire. The people are subjected to many economic disadvantages and are suffering in many ways. I believe that their ardour and morale should not be chilled further by requiring them, one might say, to sit on a great block of coal and suffer from the cold. The same may be said with regard to the town of Inverness. When the volume of coal mining was reduced, many of our miners had to go abroad. If these other seams of which I have spoken were developed, not only would something be done to alleviate the national fuel shortage, but it would mean something to the town of Inverness. Property holders who were obliged to leave the town would be able

to come home, bringing their families with them. Any way you look at the subject I cannot see why, in instances of this kind, particularly in view of the complaints of shortage of fuel, these coal deposits at Inverness and Port Hood, which the provincial government is prepared to assist to develop, should be kept closed or undeveloped on account of what I would regard as a very foolish restriction.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
In view of the resolution to adjourn having come from a Vancouver member, I feel there is the possibility of the impression going abroad that that city suffers such a climate that a fuel shortage at any time would be a serious matter, and is an idea which we who pride ourselves upon the mildness of Vancouver's winter should not allow to go unchallenged.
No one has more disagreements with some of the price control regulations than I have. But to blame them for the weather of Vancouver and the Dominion of Canada is, I think, going a little beyond what should be considered reasonable condemnation. It so happened that this winter in Vancouver, according to the Conservative paper, the Vancouver Daily Province, the temperature dropped to four degrees above zero January 22, the lowest since 1909. But by 9 o'clock on the same morning the temperature had risen ten degrees. During that period of extremely unusual weather-and it is not often we have unusual weather in Vancouver-there was a fuel crisis. Hardship and suffering undoubtedly occurred, and there was a tremendously increased demand for fuel. Steps were taken to meet that unusual situation and on February 2 the Sun newspaper reported as follows:
Army authorities to-day released figures showing a total of 690 cords of bushwood had been cut by soldiers Sunday.
Army crews continued operation at the same rate Monday and to-day, and will continue felling trees until the civic fuel committee declares the emergency over.
Shortly after that, the army that had gone into the woods to meet this emergency ceased their operations and, I presume, did so because the emergency had passed.
On January 25 the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board came to Vancouver, and of course he was faced with the problem of the fuel shortage. According to the Province newspaper Mr. Gordon is reported to have defended the part played by the war-

Fuel Shortage-Mr. McGeer
time prices and trade board in. the fuel situation and answered a series of questions relating to his organization's operations in British Columbia.
He charged that the wartime prices and trade board had received no cooperation whatever from the marketing board.
He announced that plans were already being executed for the relief of the fuel situation in Vancouver and told of measures being taken to break the potato deadlock as well. Mr. Gordon, after pointing out that logs were now being cut in False. Creek sawmills as an experimental expedient to solve the fuel problem, said that a general rationing of fuel such as had been done in respect of other products now on rations would be utterly unworkable.
The rationing of fuel in Canada, which is now proposed by lion, members opposite, would, I believe, be an extraordinary departure from the general underlying principle of rationing. True, wherever there is an actual shortage, and distribution on a basis of equality can be maintained only by rationing, all the difficulties and costs and inconveniences of rationing become necessary. But to suggest, that here in Canada, with our abundance of coal and fuel, particularly in British Columbia, we must submit to all the inconvenience of rationing, when all that is necessary is to take some reasonable precautions to see to it that an abundant supply is available, is something that I cannot support.
