speechtext:
I am not questioning the hon. member's word. I say that the force with which he presented it sent it across to me without the "perhaps." But I agree that "perhaps" rationing of everything may be necessary'.
I appreciate, and I rather congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver South upon the course he has pursued this afternoon. I would not suggest for a moment that this fuel agitation is designed to counteract the influence of the social service programme announced in the press to-day by the government. I would 72537-83-h
hardly think there "would be such a design as that, although it did seem to me, as I noticed the evident preparation of every one of the speakers who followed the mover of the motion to adjourn, that is was a fairly well-laid plan.
Coming from Vancouver, I know there are some persons there who do not believe that the government at Ottawa was responsible for the fuel shortage, and they were not Liberals.
I quote from the Vancouver Sun of February 3, which says, "Labourites demand council supply wood." And the Sun reporting the meeting of the Vancouver and New Westminster district trades and labour council has this to say:
Full responsibility for the fuel shortage was placed on the aldermen by President Birt Showier as he countered a claim by delegate Jack Price, a city council member, that the coal shortage was partly due to down-town buildings changing from oil to coal. The coal used by large buildings could not be burned in a home furnace, the president asserted. The sole responsibility for the situation rests with the aldermen and they have done nothing but pass the buck to the provincial and federal governments.
I think this incident in the house this afternoon and evening does draw to the attention of the government the nature of the responsibility that comes with bringing down any programme of controlling prices and regulating production. If the government is to control the price of coal; if the government, is to control the price of wood fuel or the price of any consumer's commodity, then the government m.ust face the responsibility of guaranteeing or taking and exercising the powers of guaranteeing the supply of that commodity at that controlled price. I mention that because I believe I have observed a tendency on the part of the wartime prices and trade _ board to assume that mere regulation of prices is all that is necessary. LTndoubtedly control of prices in this emergency is necessary. If prices had not been [DOT] controlled in this emergency, and controlled in the effective way they have been, then the disaster to those unfortunates unable to pay the price that would have been demanded would have been much greater than their suffering from the temporary shortage which existed.
I think, however, the government would be well advised to take this as a lesson, and to recognize that controls go further than the mere regulation of price. I do not think we shall ever face a serious shortage of fuel on the Pacific coast, or in Vancouver, or throughout the west. True, we may experience extraordinary weather conditions from time to time; we may face the hardship of a -temporary break

Fuel Shortage-Mr. Adamson

in, the fuel supply, but there are a great many other features of our price control that we shall have to meet as time goes on. I am not in a position to question the methods already adopted to avoid a repetition of what has happened during this winter, not only in the west but throughout the whole dominion; but if we are to make a. success of the control and regulation of prices, I think it is now fairly evident that we must also take steps to guarantee the maximum possible flow, where there are shortages, and the essential flow where there are not, of supplies of consumer needs. I do not know that to-day there is any serious shortage of fuel in Vancouver; I telegraphed to ascertain whether there is or not, but all the information I could secure before I left that city was to the effect that the situation was reasonably well in hand and that with better weather coming the emergency would pass.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had no notice whatever that this debate was coming on this afternoon. I wish to say that in reply to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer), who has just resumed his seat, as far as I know, this was no move whatsoever, political or otherwise, to counteract the valuable statement on social security which was made to-day by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie). I do not think the hon. member does himself justice in 'making the statement he made.
With regard to this question of wood I should like to offer the suggestion that we utilize the services of prisoners of war on the bush lots of Ontario. Labour with which to cut the trees on the wood1 lots is practically non-existent. I know that to be so because I live on a wood lot myself. I believe prisoners of war would be only too willing to do this work, and the English experience has been that they are of great help. When that suggestion is made, the immediate reply is that a great many of them might escape. With that I disagree. The practice has been that those prisoners allowed outside the wire are the ones who have become known as reliable people and the experience in England has been that prisoners of war have provided very useful assistance in connection with agriculture. If their work can be utilized in England, which is in a far more vulnerable and1 in a far more dangerous position than Canada, surely we could try the experiment here and see if they could be used for work of this kind in this country, for among them are many expert woodsmen.

I wish to sound a note of warning in this regard. The farmers of old Ontario know how hard it is to get wood for fuel; there is hardly a farmer who has not gained that knowledge during the past year. As a result of this shortage there will be a tendency to go into the bush lots and wood lots of Ontario and further deplete them. This would be most dangerous. I believe there are sufficient windfalls already on the ground to provide a useful supply of wood fuel for a very large part of southern Ontario, and it is this fuel that I believe prisoners of war could harvest. I would further suggest that they could be utilized for reforestation work, to be done this year and this growing season. We know we are up against it for man-power. We know we have not the man-power for this type of work, and I suggest that it would be well worth while to make this experiment in the utilization of prisoners of war.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Does the hon. member suggest that. the, farmers of Ontario would want, say fifty Germans, armed with axes, in their back wood lots?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
There would not be fifty; there would be perhaps four or five in any one place. That has been the practice in England. Could the hon. member imagine employing fifty men on one farm? They have proved eminently satisfactory and a great help ini harvesting the crop that was grown in England this year.
Then I should like to mention the danger of overcutting and further denuding our forests in the agricultural districts of Canada. In this connection I wish to quote the 'editorial from this month's American Forest, to indicate the situation that exists at present. Speaking of Europe and the warring countries, it says:
Most of these countries, even in peace-time, have to import lumber from the few nations with forest surpluses. As in England the war now is draining off forest gfowtn over a wide expanse of the civilized world. Overcutting and destruction is reported everywhere in the warring and occupied countries. Every thinking forester knows that the forest depletion that is going on in England and European countries will nave repercussions in America.
Lack of wood and the tremendous demand that is building up for it when reconstruction of these countries is at hand means pressure on our own forests. It is a fair prediction^ that this pressure, involved as it will be in international relations, may be so great as to complicate seriously and intensify our own forest problems when the [DOT] war _ is over. Skilful diplomacy will be called for in dealing with it; and that in turn will call for more exact information than we now have on our own forest situation and our own post-war needs. The one comforting fact is that we have the forestgrowing soils in abundance.

Fuel Shortage-Mr. Fumiss
This demand for farm wood, in order to keep the farm houses warm, must be scientifically administered. We cannot send the people at will into the remaining bush lands of Ontario, and say to them, "Go and cut the wood, at so much a cord." If we do that, we shall increase our problems of soil erosion, drifting and drought. There would be no surer way of causing permanent damage, damage that could never be repaired, than to allow indiscriminate, unregulated and unscientific destruction of our wood lots.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not rise frequently in the house, but I feel I should say a few words to-night to relieve the minister of the responsibility for conditions over which he has no control. The district of Muskoka, which I have the honour to represent, is one of the greatest sources of firewood in Ontario. It is within easy trucking distance of the line where coal meets wood, and the cheapness of either decides which will be used to the greater extent for fuel. .
When I tell the house that the official record of the fall of snow at Muskoka airport, in the centre of the district, was recorded two weeks ago at fourteen feet seven inches, hon. members will understand why little or no wood has been cut in that district this winter. To make matters worse, the snow came early, before there was any frost in the ground, with the result that there are some places where water stands, and on which there is no solid bottom to work. The wood was cut in the winter, and swamped out where it could be easily loaded on trucks and trucked away. That snow has settled to possibly five or six feet, and in some places seven feet.
Only recently a Muskoka resident told me that in some places in the bush of Muskoka there is a depth of seven feet of snow, and he said further that wood-cutting and lumbering is at an absolute standstill. The hon. member (Mr. Adamson) who has just resumed his seat spoke about cutting fallen timber for wood. A sawmill was located within a quarter of a mile of my home this summer. Lumber was cut out of a hardwood bush in that vicinity, and it was paid for by the thousand feet. The lumbermen took the tree only up as far as the limbs, and the result was that they left hundreds of cords of wood in the bush. That timber was cut when the leaves were on the trees. The leaves dried on the limbs, and now there is a canopy of snow over the top of the trees. That timber will lie there until the snow is gone.
I understand the subsidy is a dollar a cord on all wood cut until June 30. I would suggest to the minister that that time might be 72537-83J-E
extended in some districts until the end of October. Muskoka is not the best farming district in the world. The land is in scattered patches, and the farmer is not occupied all the summer in farming operations. He and his son, if the time were extended, could cut a considerable amount of wood which otherwise would not be cut. I know that wood cut when the leaves are on is not as good wood as that which is cut when they are off. Any practical woodman will corroborate that statement. But second quality wood is better than no wood at all. I believe honestly that if the time of cutting were extended, thousands of additional cords would be cut which otherwise would not be available for burning next winter. I ask the minister to give this matter serious consideration.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the orders of the day were called the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) moved the adjournment of the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely, to inform the house and the country of the acute fuel situation. He then proceeded to tell the house that the government had informed the country very fully on the subject some two weeks before he spoke. Then he read lengthy extracts from the statement issued by the government. It seems to me that under the circumstances he was scarcely bringing to the attention of the house a matter of urgent public importance with which hon. members; were not familiar. The advertisement from, which he quoted had been published in almost every newspaper in Canada, and in addition, radio announcements had been made calling; the attention of the public to the situation.
The government has, of course, from the commencement of the war, given'continuous attention to the fuel situation. The fuel administrator was the first appointment made by the wartime prices and trade board in the direction of the administration of an industry. That appointment dates back to 1939. The fact that nothing has been heard until recently about difficulties in obtaining fuel is, I believe, a tribute to the efficiency with which the fuel situation was administered by the wartime prices and trade board, and by the fuel administrator. I can speak freely on the subject, for it is only within the last two or three weeks that I have been directly responsible for the administration of the fuel situation. I think a splendid piece of work has been done.
We can hardly discuss coal and wood fuel as a single problem, because they differ materially. Coal is undoubtedly a national problem. It was so considered before the war, and it certainly has been so considered during
Fuel Shortage-Mr. Howe

the war. The consumption of coal in war years has increased tremendously. In the prewar year of 1939 the consumption was 29,600,000 tons. In the last calendar year the consumption was 43,000,000 tons, representing nearly fifty per cent increase. It is estimated that for the year 1943 the consumption will be 48,700,000 tons, a further very considerable increase. Of this coal only about one-sixth is used as domestic fuel. Of course the railroads are the largest single consumers, using about one-quarter of the total consumption. Heavy industry uses the remainder beyond that used by domestic users and the railroads.
The quantities of coal consumed have risen rapidly month by month, and probably will continue to rise as long a;, the present emergency exists. The production of Canadian coal unfortunately has not kept pace with the expanded consumption.' Consumption of coal . has risen almost fifty per cent in the period from the commencement of the war to date, while Canadian production has risen only fifteen per cent. Whereas Nova Scotia coal once came as far west as the lake St. John district, and Sudbury, and London and Hamilton, at the present time we find it necessary to bring United States coal as far east as Riviere du Loup. In other words, the maritime provinces production of coal is able to do little more than meet the requirements of the maritime provinces. Before the war the distribution of Alberta coal was a problem, while to-day we find that the prairie production of coal is barely able to meet the requirements of the prairie provinces. Therefore we must draw very heavily upon imports of coal from the United States. Imports of coal from England, which were very important before the war, have been reduced almost to nothing.
Last summer the difficulty of obtaining domestic coal was foreseen by the government, and hon. members will recall that an announcement was made that the government would arrange for the financing of purchases of coal by domestic users. This policy was taken advantage of to a considerable extent, with the result that far more coal was purchased last summer than is ordinarily the case. There was no difficulty about purchasing coal at that time; anyone could purchase all the coal he wished, and the financing was arranged for him by the government. I think people in general anticipated their normal requirements of coal and had that coal in their cellars. As the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Soper) has said, the dealers anticipated that the bulk of their distribution for the

year had been finished last autumn, and expected to have little to do this winter. We all know that we have experienced a very severe winter, the most severe in fifty years, and the result has been that the anticipated requirements for domestic coal have been greatly exceeded. The householder who thought he had a sufficient supply in his cellar has had to go to his dealer for additional quantities of coal.
Coal was available in Canada but unfortunately it was not always available where required, and the problem of distribution became grave. I think the efforts of the fuel controller and his staff have succeeded to a large extent in overcoming the difficulties of distribution and have put coal in the hands of users when it was required, with a very few exceptions. I know there have been threats of serious coal shortages, threats that schools would have to close, threats that families would be without heat, but I think, with very *few exceptions, the situation has been met in time, and these threatened emergencies have not actually occurred.
I do not think the problem of wood fuel can be regarded as a national problem. At the present time this country consumes about 10,000,000 colds of wood fuel. About three-quarters of this, or 7,500,000 cords, are cut by the consumers themselves. In other words, about three-quarters of the wood fuel never appears on the market. The farmer is the greatest consumer of wood fuel, and that fuel is cut by him as a normal part of his farming operations, is hauled to his house, and burned there, without appearing on the market.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31

Not the fuel about which I am speaking. I shall speak about that in a moment. About 2,500,000 cords are consumed by unban users, and this represents the marketable fuel upon which the unban householder depends. It is anticipated by the fuel controller that we shall be about 500,000 cords short of the required supply, as the situation stands at the present time. In order to stimulate the production of fuel and have it move into dealers' hands to the extent of 500,000 cords, a campaign was undertaken two weeks ago to inform the public of the situation and to offer certain forms of cooperation by this government, to municipalities, cities and dealers, in order that this threatened shortage may be overcome.
It has been said here to-day that in suggesting that the municipalities have a responsibility in the matter, the government was at-

Fuel Shortage-Mr. Howe
tempting to relieve itself of the whole problem. I think that is far from the case. In fact, I think anyone reading the announcement will take the view that the government is offering a real and active partnership between itself and the municipalities in order to solve a problem that is local rather than national. In publishing this advertisement it was the wish of the government, first, to call attention to the situation; second, to be helpful in working toward a solution, and, third, to ask each municipality to direct a cooperative effort, in line with the broad needs of the locality, in an effort to meet its own particular situation.
The offer of the government has been stated here to-day. It is to pay a bonus of SI a cord for wood cut before June 1 and in the hands of dealers on that date. The question was asked whether this $1 a cord would go to the dealer or to the producer of the wood. The SI a cord is paid to the dealer, but it is not paid surreptitiously. Every producer is advised the the dealer is being paid this extra SI a cord, and it is the intention of the government that he shall pass the bonus on to the producer. The dealers who have met with the government on this problem have all stated that it is their intention to pass on the $1 a cord to the producer, and I think I can say with great confidence that it will find its way into the pockets of the producer.

dealers were unable to operate because the price was too low. This gives the dealer a chance to operate at a price on which we believe he can operate. subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I have tried to answer it.
I did not interrupt my hon. friend when he was speaking, and I would ask him not to interrupt me.
There were some difficulties last winter in the distribution of wood, and undoubtedly there was hardship in certain areas on account of the lack of wood fuel. It was due to rather unusual circumstances. In the Vancouver area it has been the custom to depend very heavily upon what is called mill waste and sawdust; that is, the chips and shavings which are surplus from the sawmills of that area. A great many householders in Vancouver have furnaces suitable for burning mill waste and sawdust but not for burning coal. There has been a reduction in the cut of lumber in the Vancouver area, with the result that certain mills which a year ago operated on a twenty-four hour basis have been operating on an eight-hour basis, and some have not been operating at all. The supply of mill waste and sawdust was consequently greatly reduced in that area. Another difficulty was that the snowfall in the Vancouver area stopped the production of logs for a considerable period, with the result that most of the mills were closed completely for a period of some two months. That, was an interruption in the normal supply of wood fuel, which had a considerable effect in that area. Coal was diverted from Alberta into the Vancouver area to the amount of 100,000 tons. The fuel controller also arranged for the delivery of 100 million board feet of pulpwood, which was cut up into cordwood lengths and used as fuel. That very prompt action kept suffering to a minimum, but there was an unusual situation in the Vancouver area which caused hardship. The fuel controller did his best to meet that situation, and I think with some degree of success. That emergency has passed. It is to prevent exactly that kind of emergency that we are asking the cooperation of the municipalities with the government.
I have spoken of the bonus of SI a cord to dealers. The notice mentioned several
Fuel Shortage-Mr. Howe

kinds of assistance from the government. It mentioned the fact that the government would assist in the transportation of pulpwood in certain cases, where the fuel controller may think assistance is justified. The intention is to assist in moving fuel from one producing area, where there may be a surplus, to a producing area where there is a deficit. It is also the purpose to help out in trucking the wood from the roadside to destination where local equipment is not sufficient for the purpose, and to help generally in the transportation and distribution of fuel wood.
The notice also offers the help of the government in securing priorities for necessary equipment for cutting fuel wood. It also asks the farmers to take an active interest in producing an extra supply of fuel wood and undertakes to protect them against any possible violation of the war service regulations when so engaged. In other words, the notice is an offer of cooperation on the part of the government, and an invitation to local communities and the citizens to cooperate with the government in solving a problem which no section of the community can claim as peculiarly its own.
We have had various suggestions offered to-day for a solution of the problem. I think the one most often given was to increase the ceiling price. That is an easy solution for a great many problems, but it must be obvious to every member that if we were to adopt the practice of increasing the ceiling price to meet every problem that comes along, we should soon have no price ceiling and no price control at all, and thus be well on the road to inflation. Five hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party offered that solution. I urge them to avoid suggestions of that kind if they believe that price control is a sound policy in times such as this, because that policy can be maintained only by rigidly observing existing price ceilings. One breakthrough for a particular commodity invites a break-through for a number of other commodities. To maintain a price ceiling policy with frequent exceptions is an impossibility.
One hon. member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation suggested that the answer would be to pay higher wages to wood cutters. That, I think, is not a solution. The production of firewood is not an industry in the sense that it lends itself to organization on a full-time basis. It is a part-time industry. It always has been, and I think it can be operated economically only on that basis.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I made no reference to higher wages for wood cutters. I was speaking of the coal miners.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
The hon. member for Lake
Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) made four constructive suggestions. I have dealt with one of them. He made the suggestion that the government should finance the producers of firewood. I think the policy of assisting the dealer and asking the cooperation of the municipalities leaves the way open to that kind of assistance. If the dealer is not willing to finance the producer, perhaps a plan can be worked out to meet special situations, where the financing of the producer would assist in the total production. That is a matter regarding which suggestions from a local organization would receive sympathetic consideration here.
We have had the suggestion from the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Furniss) that the date be later than June 1. The reason why June 1 was set as a date is that ordinary wood should be cut by the first of June in order to be dry for use the following winter. We hope that sufficient wood can be delivered to dealers by June 1, but if later on it becomes apparent that sufficient wood will not be in dealers' hands to meet the situation, I have no doubt, that the period for the bonus will be extended.
I think that covers most of the points I wish to discuss. I ask for the complete cooperation of coal miners, producers of wood, consumers, dealers, and everyone associated with the problem in Canada. Part of the difficulties of the fuel controller has arisen from needless labour disputes. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) mentioned coal mining in his area. I happen to know that one mine in his area has been closed for two weeks over a trivial labour dispute arising out of a change of foremen. I sincerely hope that the practice of closing down this most, essential industry for trivial reasons will not continue.
One of the difficulties on the Pacific coast this winter has been the fact that what was reported in the newspapers as a slow-down occurred in the mines of Vancouver island. In the period from June 1 to date the consequent reduction in normal production has amounted to 250,000 tons of coal in that area. Surely these situations can be avoided. I am sure that the Department of Labour is doing everything it can to maintain production at normal rates. The government asks for the cooperation of those engaged in these essential industries in seeing to it that Canada as a unit puts forth every possible effort to meet this situation.
I feel that our discussion to-day has been helpful. I hope it will assist the fuel controller in bringing home to the men and

Fuel Shortage-
-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
women of Canada, both consumers and producers, the gravity of the problem and the need for action.
During the coming year we hope to have an ample supply of coal, and we hope that every consumer of coal will lay in an ample stock for the winter months. We also hope that those using wood fuel will see to it that their winter needs are supplied. If they are producers as well as consumers, we trust that they will cut a little extra to make sure that they have sufficient for the winter, and if they are dealers or producers for sale to dealers, that they will make an extra effort to see that the dealer has ample stocks in hand.
Another announcement of the government to help the situation was the offer to the dealers to buy back in June, 1944, any wood bought before June, 1943, which had not been disposed of. That, of course, is an inducement to dealers to overpurchase rather than underpurchase to meet the situation.

Coming from a district where there is a good deal of suffering, I would point out to the government that something should be done. Even if the dealers have coal, it is not possible to get it delivered. The men have been taken for the army and there is nobody to handle the deliveries. I cannot see that any appreciable progress has been made. The government can make all the statements it likes, but there are from eight to nine months in the year when we in Canada must have fuel, and in central Canada we are dependent upon the United States. We are away back to where we were during the last war, in 1917, when there was the same serious trouble. I fail to see that we are making any progress. The government is confronted with a most dangerous national problem in the present fuel situation. The first thing we know, the
United States may put on an embargo, as they did in 1917. I urge on the government that something should be done. The small dealer cannot get men to deliver fuel. In 1922 I brought this national coal problem before parliament, but very little progress has been made. We are not through the present winter yet, let alone next winter.

Mr. T. C. DOUGLAS OVeyburn): The minister dealt with a number of suggestions which were offered this afternoon, but he said nothing about the question of man-power, and that is a particularly pressing matter with reference to the coal mines. The minister said that the prairie production barely met its own needs. I can speak only with regard to the part of the province from which I come. The southern part of Saskatchewan has tremendous coal potentialities, and they are not being fully used. Last year I took occasion to draw the attention of the government to the fact that the Estevan and Bien-fait mining districts last summer were producing at about one-third capacity. Some of the pithead bosses told me that one mine normally producing seven hundred cars a month was down to about two hundred cars. A big briquetting plant which cost a million and a half dollars was completely closed for part of the year because man-power could not [DOT] be obtained. That condition was remedied to some extent by an appeal being made in the fall for farmers who had any mining experience to go in the mines. A number of them have gone there, and the situation has been alleviated somewhat. These men will be going back to the farms within the next four weeks, or even less, and the situation will be back where it was.
I was hoping there would be some statement from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) as to whether it will be possible to get labour into these coal mines. The price is not so much a problem as getting the necessary man-power. It seems to me some man-power could be found that we are not
Fuel Shortage-Mr. Mitchell

using. I have in mind, for instance, some conscientious objectors in service camps, who were working in Banff putting in ski jumps and in the Prince Albert national park putting in tourist roads. I have in mind a number of cases of conscientious objectors who are in gaol. It seems to me that there is some manpower around that is not being used very beneficially. I should like the minister to make some statement as to whether or not it will be possible during the summer to have some man-power made available to the mines; otherwise next fall we shall have the same position as we have now.

speechtext:
I will say this to my hon. friend, and the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) -will understand it better than he does: you cannot call men by phrases. Coal miners are coal miners, and we did attack this problem in a resolute way this fall. I think if the hon. member goes back to his own province he will find that we more than manned the mines in Saskatchewan last fall. We reached the point where there was an actual surplus of labour in the mines of Saskatchewan. We have 3,300 additional miners in the mines of western Canada, which is, I believe, no small achievement.
I am not afraid of the man-power situation, but I do not think it will be solved by mere declarations expressed in a few words. War in its very essence demands substitutes. Every nation engaged in this conflict will be confronted with the problem as long as the war lasts. But it can be said to the credit of the Canadian people when you view the thing in a big way on the production front-and I shall have more to say about this later in the session-when you take into consideration the agricultural production and the men we have placed in the fighting forces, the achievements of this nation, notwithstanding the opinions of some hon. members, will ring down through the pages of history. I think it far better to make a man or a woman feel that he or she is part of the war effort and that they go I Mr. T. C. Douglas.]
voluntarily where we want them to go instead of being pushed around. I have always held the opinion that you can persuade the Canadian people, but you cannot boss them too much. As far as my department is concerned in our approach to the very difficult problem of man-power, my hon. friend who comes from the old country, where they have had this background of organization of the civil services, the development of unemployment insurance, and the use of the employment offices in connection with the man-power problem of that country, w-hen he reflects on his own experiences, if he was old enough to reflect when he left there-

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Was he?

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I do not know. I do not say that in a sarcastic way. I think he will agree that our approach to the man-power problem has been a sound approach, a rational approach, and as far as my department is concerned it will continue to be so. The degree of regimentation to which the Canadian people have subjected themselves even in the last six months redounds to their credit.
At the last session we heard about labour poaching; we do not hear about poaching to-day. We heard about labour turnover; we do not hear a great deal about labour turnover to-day. I never thought I should see the day when, within six months, we should practically move the whole industrial and agricultural population of this country through the employment offices under the jurisdiction of the labour department. It may be true that in some respects the machinery is creaking a little. That is inevitable when one considers that the personnel of the labour department in the last few years has grown from practically nothing to almost 7,000. When an organization is built up that deals with the very delicate problem of moving human beings from one job to another, people who have not had a great deal of experience with that form of machinery, I think it is to the credit of the organization engaged in that difficult task, and also to the credit of the working people of this dominion, that we have been able to face up to the coal situation, to the lumber situation. I shall talk about that later this session. I feel proud of the work of this government in manning the lumber industiy of this country during last winter. I believe we have a worth-while policy, although, of course it will not cure the situation. Good heavens; look at Germany to-day 1 I have heard my hon. friend speak about organization and regimentation. Give me the power of Hitler, and I will put, not

Fourth Victory Loan
the people in this country, but the members of this House of Commons to work. They will not be making speeches here but doing what they are told. I think hon. members get my point. Even with the powers of compulsion that they have in the countries against which we are fighting at the present time there is a tremendous shortage of labour; in Germany they have to have a mass movement of the people from the countries that have been subject to their rule temporarily; they have had to pick up the populations of whole villages and put them down in Germany and set them to work.
I think our method of approach is the correct one, notwithstanding opinions to the contrary. It is largely a question of mechanics and machinery, and as our machinery gets, as I might say, more efficient-I am not taking the position that we have a perfect machine- when the people who are operating that machine gain more experience in the movement of labour in this country, they will reflect credit not only on the discipline of the Canadian people but also on the country as a whole.
